reason: The sources provide over 10 claims supported by multiple independent sites regarding the Milky Way's structure, planetary population, central black hole, and history.
story: When you look up at the night sky, every star visible to the naked eye belongs to our home galaxy, the Milky Way. For centuries, astronomers assumed our galaxy encompassed the entire universe. That view changed after the 1920 Great Debate between Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis, followed by Edwin Hubble's observations proving that other galaxies exist far beyond ours. Today, we know the Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy spanning around 100,000 light-years across, with our Sun sitting roughly 26,000 light-years from the center in the Orion Arm. At its core lies Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole with four million times the mass of the Sun, surrounded by a dense bulge 10,000 light-years wide. But the real scale breaker is what orbits those stars: with an estimated 100 to 400 billion stars, the galaxy contains at least 100 billion planets, meaning alien worlds match or outnumber stars across the sky.
angle: Our home galaxy contains over 100 billion planets—averaging at least one per star—meaning alien worlds outnumber the visible stars in the night sky.

claims.claim: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy.
The Milky Way contains between 100 billion and 400 billion stars.
The Milky Way contains at least 100 billion planets, averaging at least one planet per star.
At the center of the Milky Way lies a supermassive black hole named Sagittarius A*.
Sagittarius A* has a mass equal to approximately 4 million times the mass of the Sun.
The Sun and Solar System are located approximately 25,000 to 28,000 light-years from the Galactic Center.
The Sun is located in the Orion Arm of the Milky Way.
The central bulge of the Milky Way measures about 10,000 light-years across.
The two main stellar spiral arms of the Milky Way are the Perseus arm and the Scutum-Centaurus arm.
Dark matter is estimated to make up about 90% of the total mass of the Milky Way.
The total mass of the Milky Way including dark matter is estimated around 1.5 trillion solar masses.
In 1920, astronomers Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis held The Great Debate over the size of the Milky Way and the nature of spiral nebulae.
Edwin Hubble proved in the 1920s that spiral nebulae like Andromeda are independent galaxies far outside the Milky Way.
In Greek mythology, the Milky Way was created when milk spilled from the goddess Hera.
In China, the Milky Way is traditionally known as the Silver River.
The European Space Agency's Gaia space telescope is mapping the stars of the Milky Way.

disputed: Total star count varies between sources (100–400 billion in S1 vs about 200 billion in S5); script should cite the estimate range of 100 to 400 billion stars.
Mythological origin stories (Hera's spilled milk in Greek myth vs Marduk slaying Tiamat in Babylonian myth) must be attributed as legendary stories (e.g., 'according to Greek mythology').
